extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and students of narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling narrative point of view and methods for dramatizing a character's mind (when to use first person, third person, epistolary forms, and how to let inner life appear as action). Emphasises economy, indirectness, and techniques for making thought visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of first-person autobiographical narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: When the narrator's own life becomes the central weight of the story, a first-person autobiographical method reaches its limit: the narrator can only report and recall the past and so cannot fully present or dramatize the inner life the subject requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator is 'only a recorder, a picture-maker' and 'can only report'; his account may be vivid but would be more convincing if we could 'get behind his description and judge for ourselves.' Examples given: Meredith’s Harry (fails to dramatize his inner life), contrasted with Copperfield or Esmond where less is demanded of the autobiographer. Antipattern: relying on retrospective self-report to convey the immediacy of a character's present consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize consciousness rather than merely report it
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer making a character's consciousness into visible, enacted drama rather than letting it remain an account or reflection; 'Drama we want, always drama' for the central affair of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the chief question is 'what it was like to be X', render it 'as solidly as possible, by the most emphatic method the author can command.' Example: Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment creates the effect of the reader truly becoming Raskolnikov by dramatizing the mind; Meredith could have dramatized Harry's consciousness instead of relying on autobiographical report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use third person to present the mind in action (focalized dramatization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-person narration can return with a marked difference: instead of substituting the author's voice, the novelist can show the hero 'in the act of judging and reflecting' so that the consciousness is before the reader 'in its original agitation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method lets the character's interior life 'become visible, phenomenal, dramatic' while still permitting panoramic view and authorial freedom. Example: Henry James’s Strether is shown in the act of thinking rather than simply reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer indirect methods so the story 'speaks for itself'
rubrics_metrics.description: A prudent novelist tends to prefer an indirect (circuitous) method — retreating the authorial presence — so that the people and action appear independently, producing a straighter, more dramatic effect for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'more circuitous procedure' often leads to stronger immediacy because it places the thing itself in view rather than recalling it. The method selected should be guided by the subject of the story. Antipattern: overt authorial intrusion or explicit explanation that keeps the reader at remove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: push the method only as far as the subject profits
rubrics_metrics.description: The method should be pushed to the highest dramatic power the subject allows, but no further: if the story gains nothing from a more dramatic treatment it will be over-treated and suffer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether dramatization would benefit the subject. Example: David Copperfield did not need the highest dramatic value; turning it into a dramatized present-mind narrative would displace the subject (the linked fortunes around David) and damage the book. Rule of thumb: do not over-treat (nor under-treat) a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary/diary method as a way to dramatize feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing a novel from letters or a running diary is an attempt to show a mind 'in action' by keeping emotion contemporaneous rather than historicized; reading letters can make us 'hear the cry that was wrung from her at the moment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: immediacy, suspense, the reader accompanies the character step by step (examples: Clarissa, Grandison). Drawbacks: severe verisimilitude problems and practical strains (authors are driven to desperate shifts to keep characters always in a position to write), so use with caution and consult exemplary models for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make thought visible by representing its surface movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent the look and behaviour of thought — the impulses and reactions of mood — as the vehicle for rendering the story. The novelist can 'watch the thought itself... as it twists to and fro in his brain' and use those movements as dramatic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like a playwright uses words and deeds, the novelist can make the 'players' of the scene be the impulses of the mind. This is a technique especially applied in The Ambassadors: show the mind's 'flicker' and let it reveal inwardness without explanatory authorial comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify when a novel is 'pictorial' and requires a 'seeing eye' focalizer
rubrics_metrics.description: Some novels postulate a point of view that is not the reader's — they are 'distinctively pictorial' and require a 'seeing eye' (a selecting, interpreting, composing minister) to present the world; the story must be given as the view of an onlooker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the story 'needs' a seeing eye, use a suitable narrator or focalizer; if no such minister is needed, you may have drama unmixed (reader directly before the scene). Short pieces more often are drama unmixed; larger pictorial novels commonly postulate a seeing eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let the narrator/hero obstruct the reader's access to active mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid letting the hero or heroine come between the reader and their active mind by requiring them to portrait their own feelings unless there is a compelling effect or cause for doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle stated: 'No reflection, no picture, where living drama is possible' — exceptions only when a particular reason makes autobiography or self-portraiture necessary (examples: Barry Lyndon’s unconsciously self-revealing narration is appropriate; Jane Eyre is a special case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift responsibility from author to character for substantial fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist gains weight by fathering the fiction upon a character: 'This is not my story... it is the story of this man or woman,' which makes the fiction appear more solid and significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, this only moves the question on: the narrator still tells and the reader must accept authority. The novelist should then aim to 'get behind the narrator' by representing the narrator's mind as action rather than relying solely on their authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the subject determine the ideal point on the line toward drama
rubrics_metrics.description: For any story there is an ideal point on the continuum toward drama where the author finds the best method of telling; the choice is indicated by the subject itself and by the particular matter to be brought out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twofold consideration guides the author: (1) make the story speak for itself as far as possible (raise method to highest dramatic power the subject allows), and (2) practice economy (do not overextend the method beyond what the subject profits). Use these to choose between direct, indirect, autobiographical, epistolary, or dramatized-present methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent gradual inner change in present-minded terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When the core of the story is a gradual, internal revolution of vision (e.g., Strether's change), a retrospective account cannot convey the innumerable gradations; such subjects must be told through the character's present vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Ambassadors is 'entirely concerned with Strether’s experience' and 'never passes outside the circle of his thought'; outer behaviour and talk express only a tithe of it. Antipattern: trying to place such real inner shifts 'upon the stage' or relying on other characters' observation to communicate them.
